# AWM — agent-working-memory

> Persistent, local-first memory for AI coding agents. One Node process, one
> SQLite file, no cloud and no API keys. It decides what is worth keeping,
> returns the two or three memories that matter, and returns nothing when
> nothing fits.

**If you are a language model, read this file first.** It is written to be
ingested whole. It gives you the mental model, the setup for each situation,
the configuration that actually matters, and — most importantly — what breaks
when AWM is installed but not configured well. That last part is where almost
every disappointing result comes from.

Repository: https://github.com/CompleteIdeas/agent-working-memory
Package: `agent-working-memory` on npm · Apache-2.0 · Node >= 22
Docs site: https://completeideas.github.io/agent-working-memory/

Every number in this file is measured and reproducible from the repository.
Where a claim has a source, the source is named. Where something is unknown or
weak, it says so.

---

## 1. What it is, and what it is not

**It is** a retrieval store with a salience filter in front of it and a decay
model underneath. An agent writes short notes as it works; AWM decides whether
each is worth keeping, embeds and indexes it, and hands back the few that match
a later query.

**It is not** a vector database, and it is not a transcript log. It does not
store your conversation. It does not traverse a graph to answer multi-hop
questions. It will not make an agent remember things it never wrote down.

**The honest version of who it suits:** projects with accumulated decisions
that outlive a single session, where an agent re-deriving the same context is a
real cost. On a small or short-lived project the overhead does not pay back.
`docs/known-limitations.md` and the "Is this for you?" section of `README.md`
both say this plainly; believe them.

---

## 2. How retrieval actually works

This is the single most useful thing for you to understand, because the common
failure mode is writing memories that no channel can see.

A recall runs **three scoring channels**, then a reranker decides the order:

1. **Embedding** — `Xenova/bge-small-en-v1.5`, 384 dimensions, ONNX, downloaded
   on first use and then run locally. The vector is built from
   **`concept` + `content`**.
2. **BM25** — SQLite FTS5 over `concept`, `content` and `tags`. This is the
   only channel that sees tags.
3. **Cross-encoder reranker** — `Xenova/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`. It makes the
   **final ordering**. Its passage is built from `concept` + `content`, plus
   tags when `AWM_RERANK_TAGS=1`.

Then two things that matter less than they sound:

- **The association graph** contributes a score to about **85%** of top-3
  results but changes the top-3 **set in 0%** of them. The reranker overrules
  it; the graph's boost is capped and never wins. It is retained for the state
  it accumulates — supersede chains, causal links, co-recall history — not for
  today's ranking. (`tests/realstore-eval/graph-contribution-probe.ts`.)
- **ACT-R decay** scores every memory by age, so recall results shift as a
  store ages. Benchmarks must pin the clock or they drift day to day.

### The three consequences you should act on

- **A word that exists only as a tag is invisible to two of the three
  channels.** Tag it *and* write it in the body. Measured on a real 30k store:
  **66%** of the topical terms a memory is tagged with never appear in its
  text.
- **The reranker reads a 400-character window.** Anything past it is not seen
  by the stage that decides final order. This is not a rounding error — on the
  by the stage that decides final order. This is not a rounding error — on the
  public benchmark corpus (`npm run bench:public`, 400 probes), `s@1` is
  **97.3%** when the answer-bearing identifier sits inside the window and
  **46.8%** when it sits beyond it. Put the decisive identifier **early**.
- **Multi-hop is your job.** "Who owns the table that the failing report
  reads?" is two recalls that you make, not one traversal AWM performs. One hop
  per call.

---

## 3. Configuration that is not optional

`awm setup` installs three retrieval flags. **If they are missing, retrieval is
materially worse and nothing warns you.** This is the number one cause of "AWM
didn't find it."

```
AWM_RERANK2=1              # second-stage rerank by the cross-encoder's own score
AWM_RERANK_WINDOW=query    # 400-char window centered on the densest query terms,
                           #   instead of truncating from the start of the body
AWM_RERANK_TAGS=1          # tags joined into the rerank passage  (+7.4pp s@1)
```

`AWM_RERANK_WINDOW=query` is the difference between the reranker reading the
first 400 characters and reading the 400 characters that actually contain the
query terms. On long memories — and real memories are long, median ~1,965
characters — that is the difference between finding the fact and missing it.

**Check yours before diagnosing anything else:**

```bash
awm doctor          # reports config, live sidecars, store, and what is missing
```

If you installed via something other than `awm setup` — hand-written MCP
config, a vendored copy, a container — assume these are unset until you have
seen otherwise.

---

## 4. Setup, by scenario

Pick the one that matches. All of them end up at the same store by default:
**`~/.awm/memory.db`**.

> **Upgrade note.** Before 0.15.6 the default store lived *inside* the
> installed npm package, where `npm update` deleted it. If you are coming from
> an older version, find the old file before upgrading and move it to
> `~/.awm/memory.db`. 0.15.7 corrected the docs that still taught the old path.

### A. Claude Code, global (the normal case)

```bash
npm install -g agent-working-memory
awm setup --global
```

Restart Claude Code. **19 tools** appear. `awm setup` also writes agent
instructions into your global `CLAUDE.md` and installs hooks that checkpoint on
compaction and session end.

Flags: `--no-instructions` (skip the CLAUDE.md edit), `--no-hooks`, `--force`,
and `--no-prime`, which skips the **UserPromptSubmit prime hook** — the thing
that injects relevant memories on *every prompt*. Without it, as `awm doctor`
says, "memory reaches the agent only when it chooses to call memory_recall."
If an agent seems not to be using its memory, check this first.

### B. Separate pools per project

Not a different install — a different **agent id**. One database file, isolation
by agent. Give each project its own `.mcp.json` with a distinct `AWM_AGENT_ID`:

```
~/work/project-a/.mcp.json  →  AWM_AGENT_ID: "project-a"
~/work/project-b/.mcp.json  →  AWM_AGENT_ID: "project-b"
```

Each then gets its own namespace in the same store. See
`docs/claude-code-setup.md` ("Separate Memory Pools").

### C. Claude Code plugin

```bash
awm plugin          # prints where it is and how to install it
```

See `docs/plugin.md`. **Upgrading a plugin is not automatic** — a directory
marketplace does not pull new versions for you. This has bitten people; the doc
says so explicitly.

### D. Claude Desktop (MCPB bundle)

`npm run pack:mcpb` produces the bundle, or take it from a release. Install it
by double-clicking the `.mcpb`, dragging it onto the Claude Desktop window, or
**Settings → Extensions → Advanced settings → Install Extension…**. Desktop then
asks for two settings: **Memory database** (default `${HOME}/.awm/memory.db` —
leave it to share one store with Claude Code) and **Memory pool** (default
`work`). Restart Desktop and you should have nineteen tools.

**Sharing the store with your CLI install is the point** — Desktop and Claude
Code then see each other's memories. See `docs/desktop.md`.

### E. Server / container

```bash
awm serve --port 8400
```

HTTP API, `GET /health`, Docker recipe and Railway / Fly / Render notes in
`docs/deployment.md`. **Agent isolation on the HTTP API is by convention, not
enforcement** — any caller can claim any `agentId`. Do not expose it to
untrusted callers.

### F. Multi-agent / shared pool

Several processes against **one SQLite file** is supported and is the
interesting case: agent A writes, agent B recalls it on its next call, with no
network and no central service. SQLite WAL makes this multi-process safe.

**The thing that silently breaks it: unpinned agent identity.** If a session
does not set an explicit agent id, it lands in a per-directory fallback space
that scoped recall never sees. The memory is written and is simply invisible to
everyone else. Always set the identity explicitly, and call `memory_whoami` if
you are unsure which space you are in.

Cross-agent recall is opt-in per call via the `workspace` parameter; the
default is agent-scoped.

### G. Embedded in your own app

Import the store and engine directly — see `examples/` and
`docs/architecture.md`. `tests/longmem-eval/runner.ts` is a compact, working
example of seeding a store through the real write pipeline and querying it.

### Backend choice

- **SQLite** (default) — multi-process safe via WAL. Use this.
- **PGlite** — embedded Postgres with pgvector. **Single-process only**: a
  second process against the same directory aborts. Only for single-process
  embedding.
- **Networked Postgres** — a genuinely shared backend across machines.

Auto-detected: if `AWM_DB_PATH` points at an existing directory it is PGlite,
a file is SQLite.

---

## 5. The 19 tools

**Lifecycle** — `memory_restore` (session start), `memory_task_begin`,
`memory_task_end`, `memory_checkpoint`.

**Core** — `memory_write`, `memory_recall`.

**Correction** — `memory_supersede` (replace a stale fact; the new version
inherits the old one's associations), `memory_retract` (it was wrong),
`memory_feedback` (useful / not-useful, after you used a result).

**Tasks** — `memory_task_add`, `memory_task_update`, `memory_task_list`,
`memory_task_next`.

**Introspection** — `memory_whoami` (identity, store, backend, ports, sibling
agent spaces — call this *first* whenever anything about AWM's own state is in
question), `memory_stats`.

**Onboarding** — `onboard_scan`, `onboard_questions`.

**Output control** — `compress_output`, `retrieve_original`.

### Recall parameters worth knowing

- `granularity: 'compact'` — every result carries a ~200-char query-aware
  snippet. Saves roughly 70% of recall output tokens when you expect to scan
  several results. `'auto'` is confidence-adaptive.
- `require_confidence` — abstain rather than return noise. Default is a light
  `0.05`. **Do not raise it for ordinary recall**: a miss is expensive because
  you then go and read the codebase instead (~2,106 tokens, measured), and
  thresholds of 0.20+ cut net tokens saved by 25% in `tests/abstention-eval`.
  Raise it only for push-style use where nobody asked.
- `workspace` — cross-agent recall, opt-in.
- `limit` — default **3**, and this is a measured choice, not a guess. On 400
  real-store probes k=3 is the only **token-positive** setting: **+115 tokens
  per recall, against -680 at k=5**. It is also 41% faster at p50, because
  `limit` sizes the cross-encoder rerank pool and reranking is ~90% of warm
  recall time. The cost is ~0.5pp `success@1` versus k=5 — about 3 queries in
  400, inside noise. Raise it deliberately when you want breadth for
  orientation; leave it alone when you want a specific fact.

---

## 6. Writing so that recall can find it

Recall quality is decided when you write. Be slightly more verbose at the front
than feels natural: the head of the body is what all three channels weight most.

- **Lead with the fact or rule.** Not the backstory. "Don't mock the database
  in integration tests" first; the reason second.
- **Put the decisive identifier early** — before character 400 if you can. See
  §2.
- **Include two or more retrievable identifiers**: file paths, function names,
  column names, error strings, ticket ids. `SettlementService.closeRun()`
  beats "the accounting code".
- **Name the category as well as the specifics.** A memory about scaling an
  Azure App Service Plan that never contains the words "Azure" or "App Service
  Plan" cannot be found by them — a real miss, and the reason this rule exists.
- **Write in the vocabulary of the future question**, not your own summary of
  it.
- **Say why**, for any rule. A rule without a reason cannot be applied to a
  case you did not anticipate.

### Memory classes

- `canonical` — source-of-truth. 0.7 salience floor, never staged. Use for
  decisions, requirements, and anything other agents must be able to recall.
- `working` — the default. Findings and observations. Salience-gated, so a
  weak write may land in staging rather than active.
- `ephemeral` — decays fast.

### Content fade

Un-recalled memories gradually fade their **content** while keeping their cue
pathways — concept, tags and embedding stay intact, so they remain findable.
Recall resets the clock. Practical upshot: **do not purge memories to save
space, and do not mark everything canonical to fight fade** (canonical changes
salience gating at write time, not fade). Use `memory_supersede` for stale
facts.

---

## 7. Gotchas, in the order they bite

1. **Retrieval flags unset.** §3. Silent, and the largest single effect.
2. **The decisive identifier sits past character 400.** 97.3% -> 46.8% on the
   public corpus.
3. **Terms that exist only in tags.** Invisible to the embedding and (without
   `AWM_RERANK_TAGS=1`) to the reranker.
4. **Unpinned agent identity.** Writes vanish into a per-directory UUID space.
   `memory_whoami`.
5. **A running MCP connection never reloads code.** Rebuilding AWM on disk has
   zero effect on a session whose connection already started — a child process
   keeps the code it loaded at spawn. Restart the session, or reconnect, then
   confirm with `memory_whoami`. Do not infer the running version from
   `package.json`.
6. **Cold start is ~1.5s; warm recall is ~480ms** (measured, k=3, 11k-engram
   store, `npm run profile:recall`) — and on a genuinely fresh install, after a
   one-time **~600 MB** model download, because **nothing is bundled**: no ONNX
   ships in the npm tarball or the MCPB bundle, and all three models fetch lazily
   into `AWM_CACHE_DIR` > `HF_HOME` > `<packageRoot>/data/models`. The
   cross-encoder is **83%** of the warm figure, and its first inference is
   450-670ms of the cold one — so cold start is model load, not a slow store, and
   it is paid once per process. Never put a cold recall on a latency-critical
   path. `AWM_RERANKER_DTYPE=q8` cuts total latency **26-33%** on three suites
   for **one query in 450** of accuracy (re-measured 2026-10-09 on the shipped
   pipeline: identifier success@1 unchanged at 93.0%, topic 92.2% -> 92.0%,
   success@5 and correct silence unmoved everywhere) and it shrinks the reranker
   download from 91 MB to 23 MB. fp32 is still the shipped default. `q4` is
   dominated — same accuracy, only -3% latency, 6.1s cold start. See
   docs/recall-latency.md.
7. **The embedding model is fixed per store.** Changing `AWM_EMBED_MODEL` or
   `AWM_EMBED_DIMS` against an existing corpus leaves half the store scoring 0
   on the vector channel. AWM warns once per process; re-embed the whole store
   or revert.
8. **Invocation depends on the harness, not on AWM.** AWM cannot make an agent
   call it. If the agent is not writing memories, the instructions are the
   problem, not the store.
9. **PGlite is single-process.** §4.
10. **HTTP agent isolation is advisory.** §4E.
11. **The feedback loop has almost no signal yet** — overwhelmingly
    `useful=1`, so do not expect `memory_feedback` to be visibly improving
    ranking today.
12. **Consolidation summaries are concatenations**, not synthesis. Do not read
    them as insight.
13. **The salience filter is tuned for engineering work.** Other domains will
    need different tuning.
14. **Schema migrations are additive, not versioned.** Downgrading is not
    supported.

`docs/known-limitations.md` is the maintained version of this list, with
evidence for each item and a section of things that are **no longer true**, so
they are not re-reported. Read it before filing anything.

---

## 8. Troubleshooting

**Nothing is recalled, or the wrong things are.**
`awm doctor` → are the three flags from §3 set? Then: does the memory's body
contain the words you are querying with (§2)? Then: are you in the agent space
that holds it (`memory_whoami`)? Then: reformulate once or twice with the
domain's nouns rather than generic English. Three empty reformulations means
the memory probably is not there — go read the code.

**Memories are written but nobody else sees them.** Unpinned agent identity.
Gotcha 4.

**A code change had no effect.** Gotcha 5. Restart the session.

**"EMBEDDING DIMENSION MISMATCH" in the logs.** Gotcha 7.

**It was working and now the store is empty after an upgrade.** You were on
<0.15.6 with the store inside the package directory. §4.

Deeper: `docs/troubleshooting.md`, `docs/faq.md`, `docs/unknowns.md`.

---

## 9. Reproducing the measurements

Two benchmark paths, and the difference matters:

- **`npm run bench`** — the published numbers in `docs/benchmarks-current.md`.
  Runs against a frozen snapshot of a real ~30,000-memory store. **That corpus
  is private and is not in the repository**, so this command only works for the
  maintainer. The generators are published; the data is not.

- **`npm run bench:public:build` then `npm run bench:public`** — fully
  reproducible by anyone. Builds a synthetic corpus from a seeded generator
  (`tests/realstore-eval/public-corpus.mjs`), derives ground truth with **the
  same hold-out code** as the private path, and scores with the same runner.

**Mind the noise floor.** Two full builds differing only in corpus seed gave
`s@1` 56.3% and 52.0% — the corpus *shape* reproduces to 0.2pp and every
qualitative result holds, but the absolute moves about 4 points between draws.
A 2pp move is not a result; confirm on a second seed.

**Do not quote public-benchmark numbers as the published ones.** The synthetic
corpus scores *lower*, because generated prose is more self-similar than real
prose and same-domain neighbors are harder to separate. Use it for the method
and for deltas, not for absolutes.

Ground truth is derived by **unique-identifier hold-out**: an identifier that
appears in exactly one active memory — verified through FTS, the real retrieval
path — gives a mechanically checkable right answer. Adversarial probes are
included so that **correct silence scores positively**, which is the opposite
of what LoCoMo does. `docs/benchmarks.md` explains why LoCoMo was retired.
